title: Decryption, disclosure and detention: What the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill brings back | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 10 October 2026 00:00
-     - 11

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

A new week, a new draft law, and a new set of significant challenges.

Section 45 of the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, gazetted on 2 October, lets a Superintendent of Police, on a Magistrate’s order, direct “any person who provides locking or encryption services” to unlock a service and hand over what it holds, which is for all practical purposes section 55 of the first draft of the Protection of the State from Terrorism (PSTA) Bill returned from exile. The revised PSTA dropped that power, and its data demands on telecommunications and internet firms, after 7 UN mandate holders raised concerns about it in February. But that what the revised PSTA surrendered to criticism now, tellingly, reappears in an organised crimes statute, with a lower trigger and none of the scrutiny that attaches to the word terrorism.

Relatedly, media reported BASL President Saliya Pieris noting that the revised PSTA Bill tabled in Parliament departs in major ways from what the committee appointed to consider it had agreed, particularly on bail and on extending detention. This new POC bill also fits what I have argued about lawmaking under this Government since August, that it legislates in clusters, and in rapid succession, tabling each draft before the last has even been critiqued, migrating rights-eroding, invasive powers from one text to the next, and leaving almost no one the time, energy or the means to follow the whole.

It is exhausting, and increasingly, that seems to be very much the point.

Add the Online Safety Act (OSA), and we are faced with an unending deluge of rights-eroding, harmful legislation, asymmetrically targeting minorities, diluting dissent, all really badly drafted, and often utterly irreconcilable with existing rights protections. Civil society must read, interpret and contest each new instrument, while multilateral agencies such as the World Bank blithely fund a government that’s bizarrely fixated on rehashing Rajapaksa-era harms, risking unprecedented surveillance architectures impacting minorities, dissent, and, ultimately, democracy. 

The POC Bill borrows the vocabulary of the UN Convention against Transnational Organised Crime but applies it to domestic conduct, defining an organised criminal group as 3 or more people acting in concert over a period of time, with no need for formal roles, who aim at a “financial or other material benefit” that section 66 stretches to any advantage, “including services”. A serious crime is any of 53 First Schedule offences or anything punishable by 4 years or more, and warrantless searches, provider orders, interception and decryption need only reasonable suspicion of that, so that while a WhatsApp group does not become a criminal group because 3 people in it criticise the Government, the trouble lies in everything that happens before anyone tests it.

Old wine, new statute

The first, atrocious PSTA draft’s duty to report, punishable by up to 7 years in section 15, reappears as section 65 with a longer reach and no exclusions, requiring compliance “notwithstanding any obligation of secrecy”, whereas the revised PSTA excludes legally protected, professionally secret and self-incriminating information. Its offence of sharing “confidential information” finds analogues in sections 14 and 56, and executive detention returns too, since a Secretary to the Ministry responsible for the Police may issue Detention Orders of up to 2 months at a time and 1 year in all (section 21), with the Magistrate on first production directed to make “an order giving effect to” it (section 20(3)(a)), while Part IV disapplies the rules that bar confessions to the police, an echo of the Prevention of Terrorism Act. I can't see how the right to silence, to liberty and to a fair trial survives when professional secrets can be compelled, a Magistrate is directed to sign off on detention, and a confession given to the police is admissible in court, which leaves anyone who dissents with only as many rights as the executive chooses to allow.

To wit, where the stakes are highest, in decryption, disclosure and detention, the resemblance to the PSTA’s worst, most indefensible aspects are uncanny, and unmistakable, even if who copied from whom, and why, remains unknown. What the overlap clearly exposes is the interaction design flaw I flagged in August, which is that a power struck from one law simply moves into another, and powers refused a home in one statute seem, by devious design, to leave a forwarding address for the next. 

This is no less than democratic backsliding attempted by stealth.

Secure messaging and what encryption cannot protect

For journalists, activists, dissidents and whistle-blowers, the worry isn’t necessarily that police can break end-to-end encrypted (E2EE) apps like WhatsApp or Signal. It’s everything outside the encrypted channel – the backups, the handsets and the humans – from the cloud copy of a chat to the IT contractor who runs a rights group’s accounts. Then there’s the person at the other end of the chat, whom, incredibly, section 65 forces to tell police what they know. Section 44(4) adds that a senior officer can get who called whom, and from where, without asking a Magistrate. Anyone added without being asked to a school parents’, post-workshop, workplace gossip, gym, contemporary events or neighbourhood WhatsApp group knows how loose membership of a chat can be, which matters when “virtual meetings” with known members count as evidence of belonging to a criminal group, so that people who never knew of an investigation, and cannot challenge what they are never told, may be swept into a pervasive, invasive surveillance dragnet with no notification, no time limit, and no review.

The Anti-Corruption Act and the Proceeds of Crime Act already allow comparable orders. If the POC bill goes ahead in its current form, an investigator in the future can choose whichever statute carries the weakest safeguards. The Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) offers little refuge, since the Bill neither mentions nor displaces it and supplies no limit on purpose, no retention rule, no deletion after acquittal and no notice to the person affected. Nor will the leading social media and technology companies comply, since an E2EE service holds no keys, which makes an order under section 45 impossible to obey or an instruction to fundamentally change the product by providing backdoors. Elsewhere, all the major technology provides have threatened or chosen to exit over providing this access. Signal’s president said it would “absolutely, 100% walk” from the UK over its Online Safety Act, Apple withdrew encrypted iCloud backups from British users in 2025 after a reported demand for access, WhatsApp told the Delhi High Court in 2024 that if told to break encryption “WhatsApp goes”, and Brazil intermittently blocked WhatsApp in a long fight over court orders. Sri Lanka has by order of magnitude far less leverage than any of them, so the likelier outcome is pressure on the companies and, failing that, blocks on the platforms, as in 2018 and 2019, with ordinary users losing the means to speak, to share and to stay informed, and punished for a power that was aimed at a few suspects.

Speech, association and first principles

For Tamils in the North, already among the most closely watched communities in the country, the Bill’s idea of membership is anything but abstract, since a court may weigh “physical or virtual meetings with known members”, the “language” people use and identification “by any evidence” in deciding who belongs to a criminal group, with 5 to 20 years at stake. Going to a meeting, sending a message to a friend or using a particular turn of phrase (which especially if in Tamil risks misinterpretation by those in intelligence, Police, and related services who, by default, can’t understand or speak it) thus becomes potential evidence of belonging to a criminal group even though none of it is an offence. 

This means that the ordinary habits of association, conversation and communication that make up daily life can be gathered after the fact and read as proof of membership, leaving people unable to know in advance which of their everyday acts might one day be held against them. A ban on reporting court proceedings without permission, and on disclosing that police are investigating a group, may compound the problem by leaving a court reporter who cannot tell readers what happened in a magistrate’s court without first securing permission, or an editor who cannot confirm that police are investigating a group, so that the public learns least about the cases that most affect it. 

Layered over the Online Safety Act, the PSTA and the draconian proposed NGO law, this fails the first principles any limit on speech and association must meet, since the aim of tackling profit-driven organised crime is legitimate but the means are neither clear nor proportionate, allowing for abject fear to take precedence over competent investigation, and prosecution. 

Shortfalls against UN guidance

Sri Lanka ratified the UN Convention against Transnational Organised Crime in 2006, yet the Bill does nearly the opposite of what the UN’s own 2022 issue paper asks of a State legislating to comply. The UN paper warns that the Convention should not be used “as a pretext to eliminate political rivals, criminalise protest and advocacy or outlaw social groups”, whereas section 66 widens benefit to any advantage, “including services”, and the Bill has no saving clause. It asks for “sufficiently clear notions of participation or association”, whereas section 4(2) infers membership from language and virtual meetings, and it expects surveillance to be proportionate and notified afterwards, with undercover agents barred from inciting offences, yet sections 44(4) and 45 carry no proportionality test and the Bill has no notification and no bar on incitement.

In August I counted at least seven laws and draft laws bearing on what citizens and organisations may say, publish, fund and organise. The POC Bill is an eighth, providing insight into this Government’s true intent, since drafting this poor, vast powers this repetitive, and burdens falling this consistently on the same few are hard to put down to coincidence. Each law also makes the next easier, and all of them end up at the command of the all-powerful executive - the very office this Government promised, at the election, to abolish, but has not. The future, if the POC Bill is passed in its present form, is extremely bleak. 

I would argue that anything remotely akin to this under the Rajapaksas would have set off louder alarm bells, so that the relative quiet now is itself a measure of how much is permitted to proceed at pace, under a cosmetic veneer of ‘system change’.

title: PTSA: Realistic options | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 10 October 2026 00:00
-     - 7

The clock has started ticking on the Prevention of Terrorism against the State bill; the first of many petitions against it have been filed at the Supreme Court. Many whose prime concern is human rights appear to believe this is a bad bill. What are the realistic options before us at this moment when a Government with a supermajority has decided to pay the political price of violating its election promise to repeal the abhorrent Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) under which their own comrades suffered?

Repeal

Implementing the manifesto promise is easy. Let the private member’s motion to repeal the PTA presented by MP Shanakyan Rasamanickam in June 2026 move forward. This Act did not create any organisation that has to be wound up. The only question is what to do about the people incarcerated under the PTA and the pending cases. 

The Government has been in power for two years. It has refused pleadings for repeal and has gazetted the PTSB. This option may be ruled out.

Fundamentally revise

There is strong support for scrapping the present bill and “going back to the drawing board.” That was my recommendation regarding the Anti-Terrorism Bill that was presented by former Minister Wijayadasa Rajapaksha.  

He did not go back to the drawing board (much of that draft reappears in the present bill), but that Government did not proceed with the bill after gazetting it. As Minister Rajapaksha said at the time, the result was the continuance of the PTA. 

The Arsecularatne committee appointed by this Government has completed its work, with a few dissents such as those of Saliya Peiris, discussed below. A new committee would have to be appointed and given time to prepare a new draft when the cycle would begin again. The result would be the continuation of the PTA. 

For a Government that has gone this far, this option is unlikely.

What remains

Other than repeal and fundamental revision, three options are open to the Government.

The first is that the Government ignores civil society and the bill goes to second reading and assured enactment. The Government has the supermajority and can easily override any changes indicated by the Supreme Court, short of a referendum. Alternatively, the Government can make some changes to allow the bill to be approved in the normal manner.

A few provisions that assign powers that belong to the judiciary to the executive may draw the attention of the Supreme Court. The entirety of Section VII which subverts the Constitutional safeguard mechanism of monthly approvals of declarations of emergency by Parliament is an example. The PTA will stand repealed on the day the new law comes into force.

The second option is for the Government to bow to the outcry and withdraw the bill or keep it suspended. There is precedent in the Penal Code amendments on corporal punishment under this Government and in the Anti-Terrorism Bill of the previous Government. The PTA will continue. The President appears to have no problems in signing detention orders.

The third option is to tweak the current bill. My priorities are the changes I have been advocating which overlap with Committee Member Saliya Pieris’s dissents: “At a minimum, a judge, preferably a High Court judge, should be authorised to approve or reject the Detention Order issued by the politically appointed Ministry Secretary by amending s. 26(3) and the decisions of the Independent Review Committee should be made binding and not subject to the whims of the Minister, by amending s. 30(8).” These changes will help us pass the international-norms test needed to retain the European Union’s GSP+ concession.

It is unwise to ask for too many changes at this stage where only the Attorney General’s undertakings to the court or committee-stage amendments are feasible. Based on that assessment I limited my change requests to three: the above plus Section VII that subverts Constitutional safeguards against abuse of emergency powers. But others are free to make their own recommendations. 

Unbeknownst to the committee, it appears that their approved text has been changed. Reversing these changes may be among those done now. 

The concerns that have been raised regarding section 9, 10, and 11 may be worthy of prioritisation. The drafters have sought to reduce the bite of sections 9 and 10 (affecting communication; impinging on freedom of speech) through safeguards in section 11. But the concern is that section 11 comes into play only when the case is taken up in court. The previous behavior of Government investigators and lawyers regarding the ICCPR Act, for example, does not give comfort that they will apply section 11 diligently. By the time the person accused of committing an offence under section 9 or 10 gets the opportunity to invoke section 11, he/she would have been deprived of liberty for months, of not years.

If the third option is taken by concerned individuals and organisations and by the Government, there is no guarantee that the tweaks will be adequate. That risk is unavoidable when the power asymmetry between a Government with a supermajority and civil society is so vast. But some good may result if the third option is taken by civil society and by the Government. In this scenario, the PTA will finally be repealed.

title: Who owns new security laws? | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 10 October 2026 00:00
-     - 11

The statute in the middle will not police itself. I am the son and the grandson of two police officers who rose from the lowest rank, and I was brought up inside a police training school. What I watched, from the first parade to the last entry in the book, was a duty with a name on it. It was a grand family environment, and it is the reason I could render whatever service I have rendered. The Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, gazetted on 6 October, the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill tabled to replace the Act of 1979, and the Anti-Corruption Act as tightened this year, will stand or fall the same way. Not in the preamble. On whether every stakeholder in the circle does the one job that is his, and refuses the job that is not.

The test is whether a judge can say no? 

Three statutes are now before the country, and the argument around them has been conducted almost entirely in slogans. The Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, gazetted on 6 October, is called a police blank cheque. The Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill, sent to Parliament the same day to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act of 1979, is called the old law under a new name. The Anti-Corruption Act No. 9 of 2023, tightened this year, is treated as a side show. None of these readings is an analysis. Severity is not the test. The test is judicial independence: whether a court can refuse the power, and whether the executive can proceed without that refusal mattering.

 The missing statute

 The organised-crime bill is the most necessary of the three, and the easiest to defend if the court authority in it is real. For years, suspects in drug trafficking and syndicate crime were held under the PTA because ordinary procedure could not carry the case. The Cabinet cleared a dedicated bill on 8 September to end that practice. Minister Vijitha Herath’s distinction was the correct one. These men are not terrorists, and a terrorism file crowded with them is a professional failure. The bill gives effect to the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organised Crime. Membership of an organised criminal group for the purpose of a serious crime carries five to twenty years and a fine of up to Rs. 1 million. Detention runs two months at a time, to a ceiling of one year. Digital surveillance, interception, undercover deployment and extraction of data from devices sit under court authority. Victim identity is protected. There is no retrospective reach

 The street has already made the operational case. Police recorded 114 shootings and 60 deaths in 2025. By late September this year organised-crime shootings stood at 38, with 25 dead, leaders directing from overseas, red-notice repatriations under way and asset action running into billions. The shooter is the expendable end of the chain. The network is the facilitator, the boat owner and the man who moves the money. Ordinary procedure was written for a man caught in the lane. It was not written for a group that replaces him before the inquest is closed. A law that criminalises the group, and puts covert access under a judge who can say no, is an investigation. A law that merely lengthens custody is a round-up.

Judicial independence safeguards

 Independence is not a visit to a cell and it is not a preamble. It has four conditions, and each of these statutes should be read against them.

The first is the power to refuse. A judge who records an application he cannot reject is not independent. He is a witness to an executive act. Authorisation of interception, device extraction and extended detention must be written so that refusal is an ordinary outcome: reasons, a record, and a short appeal. Silence must not be treated as consent. On the organised-crime bill this is the feature that separates an investigation from a habit. Parliament should say so in the text, not leave it to practice.

 The second is the power to see the material. Review without the underlying grounds is theatre. A court asked to extend detention, to confirm a freeze, or to authorise covert access has to be shown why, under a procedure that protects sources without emptying the hearing. Ex parte applications are sometimes unavoidable. They are not a permanent state. The affected person, or counsel cleared to see the gist, must have a route back before the same judge.

 The third is a reviewer whose tenure does not depend on the minister whose order is under challenge. A sitting judge, or a panel nominated by the Judicial Service Commission, with reasons published, meets that test. A committee appointed by the authority it advises does not. Advice is not a decision. A recommendation that can be ignored is not a safeguard.

The fourth is a clock that cannot be reset. Detention, remand and a fresh order must not be stacked so that the statutory ceiling is a fiction. One aggregate period, one court, one record. Unannounced access, counsel and a Judicial Medical Officer are necessary protections against torture. They are not a substitute for a judge who can order release.

Where the terrorism bill still fails

The Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill improves on the Act of 1979 in ways that should be kept. A suspect is to be produced before a magistrate within 48 hours. Counsel, notice to the Human Rights Commission, medical examination and a restriction on custodial confessions are in the text. Detention is capped at one year in aggregate. Extension beyond two months requires High Court approval. A review committee is to examine necessity, legality and proportionality. These are the difference between a detention and an abduction.

They are not yet judicial independence. Human Rights Watch and the World Organisation Against Torture have marked, this week, the residuum that should not survive committee. Detention orders are obtained by the Inspector General or a Deputy Inspector General from the Defence Secretary. A magistrate cannot set them aside. Using separate provisions, a person can be held without charge for up to two years. Search and arrest on reasonable suspicion are extended to the armed forces and the Coast Guard, outside a police chain of command. The review committee is appointed by the minister whose orders it reviews, and it recommends. It does not decide.

 That structure fails the four conditions. The magistrate cannot refuse. The reviewer depends on the minister. The clock can be walked from detention to remand. Armed forces given police powers without a short handover and a police chain of command sit outside judicial sight for the hours in which abuse is easiest. Pass the law. The threat has not retired: Dalada Maligawa, political assassination, a thirty-year campaign, Easter Sunday 2019, residual facilitation and regional spillover. Cut the residuum until a judge can quash the order, see the grounds, and release. A statute where a hostile minister can aim at a rival destroys the intelligence product, because sources go silent when they believe the file is political.

The stronger model

The anti-corruption statute is already in force, and on this test it is the better draft. Act No. 9 of 2023 constituted the Commission as a body corporate that acted without direction other than from a court, and reached private-sector bribery and trading in influence. A freeze of property must be confirmed by the High Court within a fixed period. This year’s amendment adds a mandatory penalty of not less than three times the value of corrupt property, recovery of the full loss to the State, and bail only from the High Court, in exceptional circumstances, where the bribe is at least Rs. 100,000 or the loss is at least Rs. 500,000. The judicial lock on bail and on frozen assets is the point. Independence fails if the Commission is brave only against the unconnected, and it fails if a lower court can unwind a major case that Parliament has reserved to the High Court.

Every durable syndicate, and every facilitation chain that has fed a terrorist act, has rented an official somewhere: a port, a registry, a prison, a police station. Corruption is the logistics of the other two threats. A security law that cannot reach that official is half a law. The organised-crime bill should copy this discipline. Court authority that is not confirmed, recorded and open to refusal will become the rubber stamp the terrorism bill already risks.

The officer, the child, and the follow-up

The remaining duties sit around that judicial core. None of them replace it. The officer on the ground needs welfare enough to do the right thing without fear or favour: a predictable chain of command, cover for action taken in good faith inside the statute, insurance, and protection for his family when a syndicate has the address. That welfare is not a shield for fabrication, for a beating in a cell, or for a file opened to please a politician. The lines of a training school protected the man who kept the procedure. They did not protect the man who broke it. This writer was raised inside one, the son and the grandson of two officers who rose from the lowest rank. The formation was procedure from start to finish. It is the standard, not a memoir.

 The same service should own a mandatory awareness programme from the classroom to the university, with the student personally engaged rather than seated for a speech. The gang recruits where the State is absent: the school gate, the tuition class, the hostel, the phone. A child who can recognise a runner, and who has met a serving officer as a carrier of procedure, is harder to enlist. The lesson dies if the child then watches the officer taking from the gang the class warned him against. Crime prevention of this kind is cheaper than the shooting now being counted, and it is the only way the new statute does not spend the next decade processing children the last decade failed to reach.

 Rehabilitation, where diversion from a terrorism prosecution is justified, or where a sentence is served and the risk remains, should be mandatory, and the follow-up as mandatory as the order. A named officer, a family contact, a placement, and a review that can return a man who drifts. Prosecution remains for the organiser and the man with blood on his hands. A certificate without a follow-up is a ceremony. An order used to silence a critic would wreck the programme in the same stroke.

Fair scrutiny of a completed case stays. 

Malicious publication of a home address, a child’s school or a live cordon, done to intimidate or to obstruct, should be a separate offence, distinct from reporting an allegation of abuse. A ten-second clip is not a judgment. Officers who learn that initiative is punished twice, once by the gang and once by the fragment, stop making the lawful stop. Training in that environment is as necessary as the narrow rule against exposure. Diplomatic in manner, strategic in timing. Not media performance.

The standard

Judicial independence is the hinge. Without a judge who can refuse, the organised-crime power becomes a habit, the terrorism detention becomes executive custody with a visit attached, and the anti-corruption freeze becomes a headline. With that judge, the three statutes can do the work they were written for. The gang comes out of the terrorism file. The cell is met with a law tight enough to survive a hostile minister. The rented official is reached without favour. The child is formed before the network reaches him. The man who leaves a rehabilitation centre is owned after the certificate.

National security

National security is the first duty of the State. It is not a permit for prejudice, vengeance or communal selection. A law that cannot be used is a failure. A law no court can stop is a failure of a worse kind. Welcome the organised-crime bill. Pass the terrorism bill only with the residuum cut. Apply the anti-corruption law to the friend of power at the same speed as to the opponent. Give the officer the confidence to do the right thing, and withdraw it the moment he does the wrong one. Parliament’s job this month is to tell those duties apart. Anything less will be paid for in funerals, or in a service the public no longer trusts.

(This analysis is offered in the interest of national security, institutional reform, and public safety)

 (The author is a retired Senior Superintendent of Police, former head of the counter terrorism desk at the state  intelligence service, a former member of the Sri Lanka Wakfs Board, and the author of Security Beyond Enforcement: Practical Approaches for a Safer Nation (2026). Email-mahildole54@gmail.com)

title: Beyond coalition arithmetic:  Rethinking Opposition strategy after Aragalaya | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 10 October 2026 00:00
-     - 10

If Sajith Premadasa is considered unsuitable to lead the Opposition, why is his participation and the strength of the SJB regarded as indispensable to creating a credible united Opposition?

Dr Dayan Jayatilleka’s Daily FT column, “Opposition›s strategic dilemmas, Easter massacre matrix,” published on 1 October 2026, raises an important question about the future architecture of Sri Lanka’s Opposition.

Dr Jayatilleka argues that the Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB), despite being the largest Opposition party, cannot afford to “go it alone”. He contends that a “One-Party State” project cannot be defeated by a “One-Party Opposition”, that Sajith Premadasa as Leader of the Opposition must represent the interests of the broader Opposition, and that the SJB should form alliances, blocs and partnerships with diverse parties on matters of common concern.

There is considerable merit in cooperation among opposition parties when constitutional safeguards, democratic institutions, civil liberties and matters of national importance are at stake.

But there is another side to this argument.

Must parliamentary cooperation necessarily evolve into political coalition? And is reconstructing the traditional grand-alliance model necessarily the right response to the political transformation Sri Lanka experienced through Aragalaya and the elections of 2024?

This is where I respectfully differ from Dr Jayatilleka’s strategic prescription.

The Opposition is not facing a national election tomorrow

Sri Lanka is not presently in an imminent presidential or parliamentary election campaign.

This matters.

An electoral coalition may become necessary when an election approaches and the political landscape, public opinion, candidates and electoral arithmetic are clearer. But several years before such a contest, the more important responsibility of a political party may be to strengthen itself.

For Sajith Premadasa, therefore, the immediate question need not be how many opposition parties can be assembled around one table.

How can the SJB use this period to become a stronger political institution, develop a broader national constituency, establish a distinctive political identity and demonstrate that it is capable of forming a credible alternative government?

There is a profound difference between building an Opposition and building an alternative government.

The latter requires far more than assembling politicians who happen to oppose the incumbent administration.

It requires organisation, policy, discipline, competent people, internal renewal, public credibility and a recognisable governing philosophy.

The “20% bunker” requires qualification

Dr Jayatilleka argues that the SJB has failed twice to escape what he describes as the approximately 20% electoral bunker inherited from the UNP.

The electoral evidence is more nuanced.

At its first parliamentary election in 2020, the SJB secured 2,771,980 votes, or 23.90%, and 54 seats.

At the 2024 presidential election, Sajith Premadasa received 4,363,035 first-preference votes, representing 32.76% of the national vote. Ranil Wickremesinghe received 17.27%, while Namal Rajapaksa received 2.57%.

Two months later, the SJB performed substantially less strongly at the parliamentary election, receiving 1,968,716 votes, or 17.66%, and 40 seats. The NPP won 159 seats, while the SLPP won three.

These figures certainly expose a major challenge for the SJB. But that challenge is not adequately described simply as permanent imprisonment within a 20% bunker.

Sajith Premadasa has already demonstrated that he can attract well over four million votes in a national presidential contest.

The more useful question is why that sizeable presidential constituency did not translate into equivalent parliamentary strength, and how that gap can be addressed.

That requires political diagnosis before coalition arithmetic.

The local government election points to recovery

There is another electoral result that deserves greater weight in assessing the SJB’s present trajectory: the May 2025 Local Government Election.

The SJB secured 2,258,480 votes, representing 21.69% of the national vote, and won 1,767 local council seats, finishing as the second-largest political force nationally. The NPP remained comfortably ahead with 43.26%, while the SLPP received 9.17% and the UNP 4.69%.

Viewed against the November 2024 parliamentary election, the movement is noteworthy. The SJB had received 1,968,716 votes, or 17.66%, at that election. By the local government election six months later, its vote had increased by almost 290,000, while its national vote share had risen by 4.03 percentage points to 21.69%.

Local government and parliamentary elections are, of course, different contests. Turnout, candidates, local issues and voting behaviour differ, and comparisons must therefore be made cautiously. The May 2025 result cannot simply be projected onto a future parliamentary or presidential election.

Nevertheless, it is difficult to reconcile these figures with a narrative of uninterrupted SJB stagnation.

The more defensible conclusion is that, after the severe electoral setback of November 2024, the SJB demonstrated a measurable degree of recovery and retained its position as the principal national Opposition force.

This matters strategically.

If a party is showing signs of rebuilding its electoral base between national elections, the logical response need not automatically be to dissolve its political identity into a broad coalition. There is an equally legitimate argument for allowing that party to continue strengthening its grassroots organisation, improve its policy offering, recruit credible candidates and test how far its independent support can expand.

Indeed, the local government result reinforces the case for using the present non-election period for consolidation rather than premature coalition-building.

It also places the relationship between the SJB and UNP in an interesting perspective. The UNP separately obtained 488,406 votes, or 4.69%, and 381 local council seats. These votes cannot simply be added to the SJB tally and treated as automatically transferable. Voters do not belong permanently to parties. Nevertheless, the fact that the two historically connected political formations together continued to command a significant constituency strengthens the rationale for exploring a carefully structured common program before attempting a much wider and potentially contradictory Opposition coalition.

The strategic question therefore becomes even more pertinent:

If the SJB is already demonstrating measurable electoral recovery, why should Sajith Premadasa prematurely dilute its political identity by entering an all-encompassing Opposition arrangement, rather than first testing how far the SJB itself, potentially in a renewed common platform with the UNP, can grow?

The local government election does not prove that the SJB has found the complete answer to its electoral challenge.

But it does suggest that the party’s trajectory after November 2024 should be understood as one of partial recovery rather than continuing decline.

That distinction is important when determining what Sajith Premadasa should do next.

Aragalaya changed the political landscape

Perhaps the greatest danger in analysing Sri Lanka’s future Opposition is to do so through the strategic assumptions of an earlier political era.

Aragalaya changed the environment.

Whatever disagreements may exist about the movement itself, the upheaval of 2022 reflected profound public dissatisfaction with economic mismanagement, corruption, patronage, dynastic politics and the established political order.

Then came the political earthquake of 2024.

A political movement that had only three members in the previous Parliament went on to win 6.86 million votes, 61.56% of the parliamentary vote and 159 seats.

Whatever one thinks of the NPP today, one lesson from that transformation is impossible to ignore: political identity and public credibility can become more powerful than traditional party arithmetic.

The NPP did not reach 159 seats by absorbing every opposition politician available. It built a distinctive political proposition and persuaded millions of voters to move towards it.

That does not mean the SJB should imitate the NPP ideologically or organisationally.

But it does mean that the old equation of simply adding party vote banks together deserves reconsideration.

SJB votes + UNP votes + SLPP votes + smaller opposition-party votes do not necessarily equal the arithmetic sum of their previous performances.

Voters are not parcels belonging permanently to political parties.

They migrate. They respond to candidates, credibility, political circumstances and perceptions of integrity.

Coalitions can attract people. They can also drive people away.

That is one of the clearest lessons of post-Aragalaya Sri Lanka.

Cooperation is not coalition

Dr Jayatilleka is entirely justified in arguing that the SJB cannot behave as though it possesses a monopoly over Opposition politics.

But acknowledging political pluralism does not require an electoral or governing coalition with every other opposition formation.

There are several forms of political cooperation.

The SJB and SLPP may vote together against a constitutional amendment.

The UNP, SJB and other parties may jointly defend judicial independence.

Opposition MPs may cooperate in parliamentary committees, challenge legislation or defend democratic rights.

None of those actions requires a common presidential candidate, common electoral list or future Cabinet.

Issue-based parliamentary cooperation and political integration are fundamentally different things.

A mature democracy should be capable of the former without automatically requiring the latter.

The alternative to a grand coalition is therefore not political isolation.

A contradiction within the wider Opposition

There is another practical difficulty which deserves attention.

Some groups within the wider Opposition have repeatedly criticised Sajith Premadasa’s leadership while simultaneously calling for a broader united Opposition involving the SJB.

At an August media briefing, representatives associated with a Joint Opposition platform publicly described Premadasa as an ineffective Opposition Leader and questioned confidence in his leadership.

They are entitled to that criticism.

But it raises an obvious question.

If Sajith Premadasa is considered unsuitable to lead the Opposition, why is his participation and the strength of the SJB regarded as indispensable to creating a credible united Opposition?

There is a structural asymmetry here.

The SJB provides 40 parliamentary seats, nationwide organisation and an Opposition Leader who secured more than four million presidential votes.

Yet some smaller political formations want access to that collective strength while retaining the ability to promote alternative national leaders and criticise Sajith’s leadership.

Again, they have every democratic right to do so.

But Sajith Premadasa equally has reason to ask whether his immediate responsibility is to strengthen their political projects or his own.

The SJB-UNP relationship is different

Dr Jayatilleka himself recognises an important distinction in this regard.

His column argues that the UNP should recognise Sajith as leader and candidate and enter an arrangement in which the SJB is the principal force.

Here there is considerable common ground.

The SJB-UNP relationship is qualitatively different from an indiscriminate alliance incorporating every opposition organisation.

The SJB arose largely from the same broad political tradition. There remain considerable overlaps in ideology, organisation, supporters, political history and personnel.

More importantly, a process of rapprochement has already begun.

On 17 September, Sajith Premadasa publicly called for the SJB and UNP to develop a common program, describing the proposed relationship as policy-driven rather than one constructed around positions or personal advantage. Former President Ranil Wickremesinghe was present at the event.

There is therefore a credible argument for first repairing this historically divided political space.

But even SJB-UNP reunification cannot simply mean turning the clock backwards.

Post-Aragalaya Sri Lanka is unlikely to be satisfied by merely reconstructing the political establishment that existed before 2020.

The relevant question must be whether such cooperation represents restoration or renewal.

A new common platform would need new thinking, younger leadership, professional expertise, internal democracy, policy competence and credible standards of public integrity.

Otherwise, reunification may solve an organisational division without addressing the deeper political discontent that produced the upheaval of 2022 and 2024.

Integrity is political capital

This brings us to another dimension that should not be treated as secondary.

A future Opposition cannot credibly promise clean government while treating integrity as negotiable whenever coalition arithmetic becomes convenient.

This does not mean declaring political opponents guilty merely because accusations have been made against them.

Allegations are not convictions. The presumption of innocence must apply irrespective of political affiliation.

But unresolved serious legal proceedings are nevertheless politically relevant when parties contemplate formal alliances.

Consider the present circumstances surrounding Namal Rajapaksa.

On 29 September, the Colombo Chief Magistrate’s Court further remanded him until 13 October in proceedings relating to allegations of a Rs. 100 million bribe associated with the Airbus transaction. Investigators informed court that the relevant investigations had been completed and material forwarded towards possible indictment.

On 30 September, he obtained bail in a separate money-laundering proceeding relating to the Airbus matter, subject to conditions including a foreign travel restriction, while remaining in remand in the separate bribery matter.

These are allegations and proceedings, not findings of guilt.

That distinction must be preserved.

But the political question remains legitimate:

Would a formal alliance with political actors facing serious unresolved corruption-related proceedings strengthen or weaken the credibility of an Opposition seeking to present itself as an alternative political culture?

That question cannot simply be dismissed in the pursuit of numerical unity.

Do not claim integrity. Institutionalise it

Nor should the SJB respond by proclaiming itself inherently “cleaner” than every other party.

Such claims are subjective and vulnerable to contradiction.

The stronger approach would be to institutionalise integrity.

A future SJB-UNP common platform could establish objective standards relating to asset declarations, conflicts of interest, campaign finance, candidate vetting, procurement interests, serious criminal proceedings and codes of public conduct.

The standards should apply equally to SJB members, UNP members and anyone seeking to join from another political formation.

That would transform the discussion.

The message would no longer be: “Our politicians are good; your politicians are bad.”

It would become: “Everyone participating in this political project must satisfy the same publicly declared standards.”

That is a much stronger foundation for political credibility.

Build the platform before building the coalition

There is therefore another model available to the Opposition.

First, allow the SJB to strengthen its own organisation and political identity.

Second, consolidate the historically divided SJB-UNP political space around an agreed program.

Third, establish transparent standards of governance, integrity and candidate selection. Fourth, open that platform to credible political figures, professionals, younger leaders and others from across the country who accept those principles.

A broader Opposition can then emerge organically around a recognisable political project.

This reverses the conventional coalition model.

Instead of asking: “Which party leaders must Sajith accommodate?” the question becomes: “Who is willing to subscribe to the principles, program and standards of a credible alternative government?”

Individuals from other opposition parties should not be excluded simply because of their political origins.

There are undoubtedly experienced, competent and principled people across Sri Lanka›s political spectrum.

But neither should entire political organisations, leadership structures and historical liabilities automatically be absorbed merely because they currently oppose the NPP.

A broader coalition can develop later, when circumstances require it.

There is no strategic necessity to import every piece of political baggage today.

Sajith’s political identity

This may ultimately be Sajith Premadasa’s most important challenge.

He already occupies the constitutional position of Leader of the Opposition.

But leadership of the Opposition and leadership of an alternative government are not synonymous.

The latter must be earned through public confidence.

The task is therefore not merely to inherit everyone who opposes the NPP.

It is to define what the SJB represents.

Is it social democratic?

Is it committed to a competitive market economy with strong social protection?

What are its standards on corruption?

How will it reform the State?

How will it govern differently?

How will it bring professionals and younger people into decision-making?

How will it strengthen democratic institutions while avoiding the patronage systems of the past?

Those questions matter more today than determining which opposition politician stands on which platform three years before a national election.

Two competing theories

Ultimately, the debate with Dr Jayatilleka concerns two different theories of political consolidation.

One is coalition arithmetic.

Fragmentation weakens the Opposition, therefore opposition parties must combine.

The other is credibility-first consolidation.

First establish political identity, organisational strength, integrity standards and a compelling governing program. Then allow broader political consolidation to develop around that foundation.

Neither guarantees electoral victory.

And circumstances closer to an election may require compromises that cannot be predicted today.

But Aragalaya and the extraordinary voter movements of 2024 suggest that the second theory deserves far more serious consideration than traditional political arithmetic permits.

The fundamental problem confronting Sri Lanka’s Opposition may not simply be that it is fragmented.

The deeper problem may be that large sections of the electorate remain sceptical of the traditional political establishment itself.

If that diagnosis is correct, merely recombining the components of that establishment will not necessarily constitute political renewal.

Sajith Premadasa therefore does not have to choose between isolation and indiscriminate unity.

There is a third path.

Strengthen the SJB.

Rebuild the historically divided SJB-UNP political space on a genuinely renewed basis.

Protect a distinctive identity through objective standards of integrity and governance.

Cooperate with every democratic party where the national interest, Constitution or parliamentary process requires it.

And allow a broader alternative to grow around a credible political platform rather than assembling a coalition merely because its members share a common opponent.

The question for Sri Lanka’s Opposition is therefore larger than who can be brought together against the NPP.

What kind of political alternative can persuade a post-Aragalaya electorate that Sri Lanka is being offered something genuinely different from the political culture it rejected?

That, more than coalition arithmetic, may define the next phase of Opposition politics.

(The author is Senior Advisor to Sajith Premadasa on Strategic and Policy Affairs and Principal Advisor on Environmental and Wildlife Conservation).

title: Myth of Tarshish: Was Galle truly King Solomon’s lost port? | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 10 October 2026 00:00
-     - 8

The Visit of the Queen of Sheba to King Solomon painting by Edward Poynter 

(Wikimedia Commons)

Mural at Colombo Port Maritime Museum (Avi Kumar)

Galle Lighthouse (Avi Kumar)

For over a century, the claim that the port of Galle was the biblical port of Tarshish—King Solomon’s legendary trade hub—has lingered in local rumours, tourist brochures, and newspapers. However, a glance into the evidence shows that this rumour is incredibly difficult to verify, no matter how romantic it sounds.

Popularised by former Colonial Secretary Sir James Emerson Tennent in 1859, this unproven theory has been repeated so often that many locals and tourists alike take it as undisputed fact. Yet the colonial myth is not supported by archaeology, linguistics, geology, or logistic evidence. The most glaring flaw is simple arithmetic. King Solomon reigned around 970-931 BCE. Sri Lanka’s first historic king, Vijaya, did not arrive until roughly 500 BCE and the sprawling markets of the Anuradhapura Kingdom emerged much later.

In 1 Kings 10:22, the Bible states that Solomon’s  fleet returned once every three years bearing a specific luxury cargo: “Gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.” 

Colonial European theorists in the age of empires scrambled to find an island capable of supplying this exotic inventory. 

Had ancient Israelite sailors landed in Galle during Solomon’s era, they would not have stepped onto a bustling cosmopolitan dock; instead, they would have encountered hunter-gatherer communities. True, the island was not entirely isolated. Excavations by Senior Professor Raj Somadeva have uncovered human activity and Iron Age civilisations in highland cave sites dating back to 1000 BCE, predating King Vijaya. His discoveries of marine shark teeth and coastal corals deep in the interior highlands confirm that early Sri Lankans engaged in domestic barter between the coast and mainland. Yet, maintaining supply-chains with far away kingdoms is far more complex. 

The island lacked the highly organised royal infrastructure, holding complexes, or networks required to capture, cage, domesticate, and export hundreds of live monkeys and wild birds. While the later Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa kingdoms had advanced royal pleasure gardens and elephant taming techniques, they emerged centuries afterwards. Furthermore, Galle did not appear on global records until the Greek geographer Ptolemy mentioned it around 150 CE, then it gained prominence only during 16th-century conflicts with the Portuguese Empire.

Even if the local tribes of the era had somehow cornered the market on caging wild primates, logistics would fail them. Transporting hundreds of fragile, highly stressed tropical animals across the scorching, open wooden decks of an ancient merchant galley—while navigating the stagnant summer air of the Arabian and Red Seas and subsequent camel caravan routes—would result in many exotic jungle critters dying before reaching the pet markets or menageries of ancient Jerusalem.

The linguistic “proof” that 19th-century colonial theorists leaned so heavily upon—the similarity between Biblical Hebrew and South Asian words cannot be verified. They linked the Hebrew word for ape (kophim) to the Tamil and Sanskrit kapi, and the word for peacock (tukkiyim) to thogai, the Tamil word for a peacock’s tail. However, it is far more plausible that these maritime loanwords simply spread fluidly and indirectly across the ancient world from one trading group to another. In fact, there is a closer alternative: Ancient Egypt. The word kophim is similar to the Egyptian word gif (vervet monkey). Meanwhile, tukkiyim could alternatively stem from the Egyptian word tekh, referring to African sacred ibis. 

Furthermore, the colonial theory is rife with zoological and semantic flaws. First, Sri Lanka lacks apes; it only has monkeys. Second, in modern Israeli Hebrew, the word tuki (derived from tukkiyim) means “parrot” 

 not peacock. The classical Hebrew spoken during King Solomon’s era went extinct as a spoken language for centuries. By the time Jesus was born 900 years later, it was a dying language and it wasn’t Jesus’s first language. When Hebrew was recently revived by European Jewish scholars, the exact meanings and context of many ancient words had already been lost. So, trying to match words for animals across languages is probably not the most accurate way to map ancient sea routes. 

Scholars also ponder if “ships of Tarshish” was ever a geographic destination at all, but rather a term for a class of large, ocean-faring ships.

The biblical text also mentions ivory. While Mediterranean islands like Cyprus had prehistoric dwarf elephants and Crete had dwarf mammoths - both were extinct by Solomon’s time. You cannot carve mineralised stone fossils like fresh ivory. Interestingly, the large hole in these fossilised skulls where the trunk should be later inspired legends of the one-eyed Cyclops (but that’s another story). Instead of sailing to Asia, Near Eastern kings had access to thriving wild populations of now-extinct Syrian and North African elephants.

In the Book of Ezekiel, Tarshish is described as a metal hub, trading in iron, silver, tin, and lead. Sri Lanka completely lacks major deposits of these metals (except iron). Why would King Solomon send a fleet across the globe to import metals from an island that would, centuries later, have to import those very same materials just to forge its own coins and bronze statues? Ancient Sri Lanka, by contrast, built a reputation on luxury commodities: blue sapphires, gems, pearls, and high-quality cinnamon.

And the Bible verse also points us entirely in the opposite direction. When the Prophet Jonah boarded a ship at Jaffa to flee the wrath of God, he headed west across the Mediterranean toward Tarshish—possibly aiming for the Phoenician mining colonies in Europe. This also corresponds with other hypothetical locations—such as Tartessos in Spain or Carthage in North Africa—also being debated.

How, then, did Sri Lankan cinnamon end up in ancient Israeli sites like Tel Dor and in Egyptian mummies? It seems more likely that trade happened via overland and maritime middlemen rather than direct shipping. Phoenician merchants fiercely protected their supply chains. To prevent competitors from discovering their sources and to artificially inflate prices, they invented far-fetched myths to superstitious and gullible customers. They told the buyers tall tales, claiming that the exotic items were harvested from dragon-guarded valleys or taken from giant phoenix nests. They swore they had to navigate phantom currents infested with bloodthirsty mermaids who lured crews down into watery graves. The truth is that the location of the exotic merchandise remained a heavily guarded corporate secret, shrouded in secrecy among a vast network of middlemen.

Furthermore, in Solomon’s Empire, ancient Israelites and Jews were not the majority; they were a ruling minority over Canaanites, Hittites, Jebusites, and other groups. Solomon married many wives from these groups to consolidate political power. The Israelite tribe of Dan and the Phoenicians were the communities that dominated marine trade. Therefore, even if Solomon the Wise’s subjects made a brief cameo on the tropical island, they would not necessarily have been the historical forerunners to modern Jewish communities. 

Ancient Israelites are not mentioned in classical ancient Sinhala chronicles or religious texts like the Mahavamsa, Culavamsa, or Dipavamsa, and early records of Jewish presence by foreign visitors much later remains scant and no ancient synagogues or Jewish burial sites have been found. But does Sri Lanka have to inherit the myths of other civilisations to secure its prestige? When it has developed a unique destiny of its own and just as elegantly written in the history books. Other rumours such as the Thattar community or Rodiyas having Jewish origins have also been cited in recent discussions but similarly stand unproven. 

The Tarshish theory is a relic of colonial-era romanticism that looks at the past through a Western lens. While historians will debate and continue to try and unravel this mystery, perhaps the past does not need to be perfectly decoded to be magnificent. The true grandeur of this mystery lies in the fact that some fragments of history may just lie hidden in the depths of the sea, lost to time and tide.

title: Beyond “Cosmic Myth”: Buddhism, history and search for inclusive Sri Lankan Republic | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 10 October 2026 00:00
-     - 11

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake speaks with some of the venerable monks who attended a meeting on Thursday

I read Sarath de Alwis’s “Ghost of Gnanasara haunts our republic” (https://www.ft.lk/columns/Ghost-of-Gnanasara-haunts-our-republic/4-798359) with respect for the author’s long experience as a journalist and his evident concern about the future of Sri Lanka. His right to question religious institutions, political establishments and historical narratives is beyond dispute. A democratic society must protect that freedom.

But freedom to question does not require us to accept every interpretation offered in its name. I believe some of the historical conclusions in the article deserve closer examination, particularly where documented history, scholarly interpretation and rhetorical assertion appear to merge.

There is no reason to deny that Buddhist institutions in Sri Lanka have experienced caste distinctions, political patronage, struggles over authority and disputes concerning property. These are legitimate subjects for historical inquiry.

The history of the Siyam Nikaya is a good example. Higher ordination was restored in 1753 through monks brought from Siam, with the support of King Kirti Sri Rajasinghe and Weliwita Saranankara. Subsequently, higher ordination within the Siyam Nikaya became restricted to Govigama candidates. This exclusion was historically significant and contributed to the emergence of the Amarapura and Ramanna fraternities.

That history should neither be concealed nor romanticised.

But neither should it be simplified. To describe the Siyam Nikaya merely as a “deliberate instrument of feudal statecraft” is an interpretation, not an uncontested historical fact. Religious revival, royal patronage, monastic reform, caste interests and political authority were intertwined. Reducing that complex historical process to political engineering risks replacing one simplified narrative with another.

The same caution applies to the British period.

The Kandyan Convention of 1815

The Kandyan Convention of 1815 unquestionably gave Buddhism a privileged constitutional position. The British undertook to protect and maintain the Buddhist religion, its rites, ministers and places of worship. That is historical fact.

British colonial policy towards Buddhism, however, was considerably more complicated than a simple bargain in which the colonial rulers protected monastic landlords in return for political obedience. British administration simultaneously protected, regulated and transformed Buddhist institutions. Questions of monastic property, succession and institutional authority increasingly became subject to colonial law and courts.

Consequently, the assertion that the British protected monastic property so that monks could “keep the populace subdued and loyal to the status quo” should be regarded as a political interpretation requiring evidence, rather than as an established historical conclusion.

There is an even more fundamental distinction that shouldnot be lost in this debate:

Buddhism is not synonymous with Sinhala-Buddhist nationalism.

There is abundant historical evidence that Buddhism became intertwined with Sinhala nationalism, particularly during the late colonial and post-colonial periods. Religious identity, ethnicity, historical memory and political mobilisation have at various times reinforced one another. This deserves serious and sometimes severe criticism.

But criticism of Sinhala-Buddhist nationalism is not the same thing as criticism of Buddhism itself.

The ethical teachings of Buddhism—Metta (loving-kindness), Karuna (compassion), Ahimsa (non-harming), truthfulness, generosity, restraint and the purification of the mind—cannot simply be reduced to an ideology of ethnic supremacy.

Indeed, Buddhist teachings provide grounds for criticising Buddhists when their conduct contradicts those principles.

A Buddhist institution can fail to live according to Buddhism. A Christian institution can fail to live according to Christianity. A political party can betray its declared principles. The failure of an institution should not automatically be treated as proof that the philosophy itself is fraudulent.

This distinction matters greatly in Sri Lanka.

We should be able to acknowledge historical discrimination committed in the name of Buddhism without condemning Buddhism itself. We should acknowledge the privileges historically enjoyed by the Sinhala majority without treating every Sinhala person as an ethnonationalist.

We should recognise the grievances of minorities without permanently defining them through victimhood. We should criticise political monks when their conduct deserves criticism without portraying the entire Sangha as a political conspiracy.

Above all, the rule of law must apply equally.

A monk is a citizen. A politician is a citizen. A journalist is a citizen. A businessman, priest, teacher or ordinary citizen is equally a citizen. No robe, office, wealth, ethnicity or religious affiliation should place anyone above the law.

But defending equality before the law does not require treating Buddhism as an obstacle to democracy.

Political order 

Sri Lanka’s challenge is not to choose between Buddhism and democracy, or between Sinhala culture and pluralism. Our challenge is to construct a political order in which religious conviction and equal citizenship can coexist without one becoming a weapon against the other.

This is why I am uncomfortable with the broad use of the phrase “cosmic myth” to describe the historical foundations of Sinhala-Buddhist identity.

Every civilisation possesses narratives of origin, belonging, sacrifice and continuity. Some are historically verifiable; others are religious or cultural traditions; many contain elements of both.

The proper response is not to replace one community’s mythology with another community’s counter-mythology.

The proper response is historical literacy.

We should learn to distinguish between what is documented, what is disputed, what is scholarly interpretation and what is political rhetoric. Such discipline is particularly important in a country where careless words can deepen wounds that have already cost us enormously.

The same principle applies when invoking great thinkers. Albert Einstein’s complex attitude towards religion, for example, cannot responsibly be reduced to a convenient quotation proving either belief or unbelief. He rejected belief in a personal God while retaining a profound sense of wonder about the universe and what he regarded as the spiritual dimension of human existence.

Great thinkers should be studied, not recruited as weapons for contemporary arguments.

Sri Lanka now needs precisely this intellectual maturity.

Future of Sri Lanka 

We must create a republic in which a Buddhist does not have to surrender his or her faith to be a good citizen; where a Hindu, Muslim or Christian does not have to apologise for his or her identity; and where an atheist or agnostic enjoys precisely the same citizenship as a believer.

That is not a compromise. It is the essence of equal citizenship.

The future of Sri Lanka should therefore not be a contest between competing historical or “cosmic” narratives. Nor should the answer to the excesses of religious nationalism be an equally intolerant secularism that regards religious identity itself as a problem.

We need something more difficult and more mature: a civic order capable of accommodating our differences while holding firmly to one principle—that no citizen is above the law and no citizen is below the law.

I therefore respectfully disagree with Sarath de Alwis where historical complexities appear to be transformed into sweeping conclusions about Buddhism, the Sangha and Sinhala identity. At the same time, I defend his right to make those arguments.

That is precisely the kind of Sri Lankan republic I hope we can build: one in which historical truth is pursued without hatred, religion is practiced without domination, criticism is expressed without dehumanisation, and citizenship is never determined by race, religion or political allegiance.

Our task is not to destroy one another’s histories.

It is to learn how to live together despite them.

That, ultimately, may be the most important lesson Sri Lanka can draw from its long and difficult history.

Sri Lanka’s sporting community has been plunged into grief following the tragic death of para-shooter Niranjala Ranasinghe, who passed away on October 5, 2026, following a sudden accident.

The National Paralympic Committee of Sri Lanka expressed profound sadness over her untimely death, paying tribute to an athlete whose dedication, courage and commitment to representing her country will always be remembered.

Ranasinghe was preparing to represent Sri Lanka at the fifth Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, scheduled to be held from October 18 to 24. She was named as the sole representative of Sri Lanka in para-shooting for the continental competition, where she was set to compete in the 10m air rifle events.

Her selection for the Games marked a significant milestone in her sporting career, reflecting her determination to compete at the highest level of international para-shooting.

Ranasinghe had gained valuable international exposure through participation in major qualifying competitions, including the World Shooting Para Sport World Cup in New Delhi, India, and the Para Shooting World Championships in South Korea and Jordan. These international appearances provided her with opportunities to compete against experienced shooters and develop her skills on the global stage.

In the 10m air rifle discipline, para-athletes require exceptional concentration, precision, consistency and composure under pressure. Ranasinghe’s participation in international competitions demonstrated her commitment to pursuing excellence and earning the opportunity to represent Sri Lanka at major sporting events.

Her Asian Para Games campaign was expected to be another important chapter in her sporting journey. She was due to compete in the R2 Women’s 10m Air Rifle Standing and R3 Mixed 10m Air Rifle Prone events under the World Shooting Para Sport classification system.

However, her sudden passing has tragically ended her dream of competing in Japan and wearing the Sri Lankan national colours at one of Asia’s premier multi-sport events.

As Sri Lanka prepares for the Games, her absence will be deeply felt by fellow athletes, coaches and officials. Her story reflects the courage, perseverance and determination of para-athletes who overcome challenges in pursuit of sporting excellence.

The National Paralympic Committee extended its heartfelt condolences to her family, friends and all those who supported her sporting journey.

Though she will not have the opportunity to compete at Aichi-Nagoya, Niranjala Ranasinghe’s commitment to representing Sri Lanka will remain a poignant part of the nation’s para-sporting story. May she rest in peace. (HW)

title: Farhan leads Pakistan to victory on debut as Captain | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 10 October 2026 00:00

Lahiru Udara celebrates his maiden T20I fifty

Naseem Shah struck in the first over on his way to three wickets

Sahibzada Farhan scored a fifty on his debut as Pakistan T20I Captain

Maaz Sadaqat scored a rapid 50 off 

29 balls

RAWALPINDI: Sahibzada Farhan in his debut as T20I Captain guided Pakistan to a four-wicket win over Sri Lanka in the first T20I played at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Friday to put his team 1-0 up in the three-match series.

Farhan struck 10 fours and 4 sixes in his knock of 89 off 53 balls as Pakistan chased down Sri Lanka’s total of 182-8 to win with seven balls to spare.

Farhan starred in partnerships of 54 off 31 balls for the first wicket with Fakhar Zaman (21) and 92 off 52 balls with 21-year-old newcomer Maaz Sadaqat who virtually took the game away from Sri Lanka with a blistering 50 off 29 balls (4 fours, 3 sixes).

Sri Lanka fought back after the partnership was broken to capture five wickets for 34 runs, but Pakistan by then were not under any pressure to score the remaining runs.     

Sri Lanka winning the toss and choosing to bat first finished on 182-8 with half of their runs coming from the bat of Lahiru Udara. The ball moved around early and Sri Lanka struggled against the Pakistan seamers after opting to bat. Captain Kusal Mendis fell early while Kamil Mishara, who walked in after his dismissal, took nine balls to get off the mark. If not for Udara, Sri Lanka might have struggled to put up a score on the board.

Udara struck a magnificent 91 off 55 deliveries (11 fours, 1 six) as he almost single handedly dragged his side into this contest. There were crucial stands of 60 off 37 balls and 57 off 34 balls between Udara and Kamindu Mendis (23) and Udara and Dasun Shanaka (18). Those stands helped set a pretty handy platform for the death overs, but Sri Lanka’s lack of lower order power hitting meant they weren’t full able to capitalise on the death overs - managing 41 runs across the final four.

Udara was brilliant with his footwork against the spinners, moving around in the crease, never allowing them to settle down. He used the pace of Razaullah quite nicely. One thing Pakistan will be really disappointed about will be the 18 wides they gave away, nearly all of them by Naseem Shah. Sri Lanka will also be grateful for the 29 extras offered up. 

Pakistan›s effort was spearheaded by debutant Muhammed Imran, who finished with exceptional figures of 2/21, but the rest of the bowlers all received some stick courtesy Udara.
